title: Subqueries
subtitle: Nested SELECT — scalar, IN, EXISTS, and derived tables
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Some questions require multiple steps: 'Find products more expensive than the average.' You need to compute the average first, then compare. Joins can't express this directly.
whyItExists.solution: A subquery is a SELECT inside another SELECT. The inner query runs first and provides its result to the outer query. Subqueries can appear in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and HAVING.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Multi-step logic: compute then compare, filter using aggregated results, find rows based on related rows in another table.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When a JOIN or CTE would be clearer. Correlated subqueries run once per outer row — can be slow. Prefer a JOIN or window function for performance at scale.

explainModes.beginner: A subquery is a query inside a query. Think of it as answering a smaller question first, then using that answer in the bigger question. 'Find products more expensive than average' = first ask 'what IS the average?', then compare each price to it.
explainModes.simple: Scalar subquery: (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products) — returns one value, used in SELECT or WHERE. IN subquery: WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders) — matches any returned value. EXISTS: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id) — true if any rows match. Derived table: FROM (SELECT ...) AS alias — subquery in FROM.
explainModes.standard: Scalar subquery must return exactly 1 row and 1 column or it errors. Uncorrelated subquery runs once. Correlated subquery references the outer query and runs once per outer row — slow on large tables. EXISTS short-circuits on first match (efficient). NOT EXISTS is the anti-join pattern. Subquery in SELECT: SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id = u.id) AS order_count FROM users u — correlated scalar subquery.
explainModes.technical: The optimizer can often unnest (inline) subqueries and convert them to equivalent JOINs for better plans. EXISTS is implemented as a semi-join. NOT IN with NULLs is a trap — if the subquery returns any NULLs, NOT IN returns no rows (NULL-comparison issue). Use NOT EXISTS instead. Derived tables (subquery in FROM) create temporary result sets — now superseded by CTEs (WITH clause) for readability.
explainModes.deepDive: Lateral subqueries (LATERAL keyword) allow the right-side subquery in FROM to reference columns from tables to its left — they run per row. Not available in all databases; SQLite 3.41+ supports it. For top-N per group, LATERAL + ORDER BY LIMIT is clean and efficient. The Unnest() function with LATERAL is a common PostgreSQL pattern for expanding arrays into rows. Materialized CTEs (WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED) force the optimizer to compute the CTE once.

content.code:
-- Scalar subquery: returns one value
-- Products more expensive than the average
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);

-- Scalar subquery in SELECT column
SELECT
    name,
    price,
    ROUND((SELECT AVG(price) FROM products), 2) AS avg_price,
    price - ROUND((SELECT AVG(price) FROM products), 2) AS diff_from_avg
FROM products;

-- IN subquery: users who have placed at least one order
SELECT name, city
FROM users
WHERE id IN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders);

-- NOT IN: users who have NEVER ordered
SELECT name, city
FROM users
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);

-- EXISTS: efficient, stops on first match
SELECT name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND o.total > 1000
);
-- 'Give me users who have at least one order over 1000'

-- NOT EXISTS (preferred over NOT IN)
SELECT name
FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id
);

-- Derived table: subquery in FROM
-- Find users whose average order exceeds 500
SELECT u.name, avg_orders.avg_total
FROM users u
JOIN (
    SELECT user_id, ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_total
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY user_id
) AS avg_orders ON u.id = avg_orders.user_id
WHERE avg_orders.avg_total > 500;

questions.question: What is the risk of using NOT IN with a subquery that might return NULL values?
options: If the subquery returns any NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all
It only matters for text columns
questions.explanation: NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is equivalent to NOT (id=1 OR id=2 OR id=NULL). Since id=NULL evaluates to NULL (not FALSE), the entire NOT expression evaluates to NOT NULL = NULL for every row — so nothing passes the filter. Use NOT EXISTS to avoid this trap.

faq.q: When should I use a subquery vs a JOIN?
faq.a: JOINs are usually faster and more readable for combining rows from related tables. Use subqueries when you need to compute something first (scalar subquery for averages/counts), use IN/EXISTS for existence checks, or build derived tables for intermediate aggregations. When a subquery gets complex, convert it to a CTE (WITH clause) for readability.

examples: WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products WHERE category = 'Electronics') — above-category-average items
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments WHERE payments.order_id = orders.id) — unpaid orders
FROM (SELECT user_id, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY SUM(total)) AS quartile FROM orders GROUP BY user_id) — customer segmentation
